analysis.one_liner: Caps federal farm subsidy payments at $35,000 per person and closes loopholes letting big operators collect multiple payments.
analysis.headline: The Farm Fairness Act was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in October 1995, received no cosponsors, and never got a committee action or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have tightened the cap on federal farm subsidy payments, limiting any one person to $35,000 a year across the major commodity programs for wheat, feed grains, cotton, rice, and oilseeds. It would have attributed payments from corporations, partnerships, and joint ventures directly to the people who own them, ending the rule that let one operation qualify as up to three separate "persons" and collect up to three sets of payments. It also tightened who counts as "actively engaged in farming" — requiring real, substantial labor or management to qualify — and lengthened the ineligibility penalties for schemes or fraud.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who fund commodity subsidy payments and would pay less under tighter caps; and small and mid-sized family farms, which typically collect payments below the cap and compete with large operations that today can multiply their payments across multiple entities.

how_it_helps.text: Caps total commodity program payments (deficiency, loan deficiency, diversion, and related payments) at $35,000 per person per year, down from limits that large operations could multiply through entities.

Attributes payments received by any entity to the individuals who own it, in proportion to ownership, and eliminates the "three entity rule" that let one operation qualify as up to three separate persons for payment purposes.

Subject partnerships and joint ventures to the same payment limit and tightens "actively engaged in farming" rules, requiring stockholders or members owning at least half the operation to contribute significant personal labor or on-site management, with payments reduced for absentee owners who do not.
Lengthens the ineligibility penalty for "scheme or device" violations to six crop years, and to eleven years when fraud was involved, strengthening enforcement against program abuse.

analysis.who_pays: Large commodity producers — big grain, cotton, and rice operations and investors in farm partnerships and corporations — who would see their subsidy payments capped and could no longer multiply payments through multiple entities or qualify with only minimal involvement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large agribusiness and absentee farm investors

drawbacks.text: Tighter "actively engaged in farming" tests could burden genuine family farm corporations going through succession; the bill acknowledges this by including a 10-year transition rule for family corporations that lose eligibility because of a stockholder's death, disability, or retirement.

Lower subsidy caps can leave large producers with less income support in bad price years, which supporters of unlimited payments argued could stress farm-dependent rural economies — a cost borne mainly by the largest operations but felt in farm communities.
The stricter definition of active personal management (daily, on-site involvement) would exclude some owners who contribute real but less hands-on management, reducing payments they receive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main effect is a straightforward one: less federal money flowing to the largest subsidy recipients. The costs fall on large operations and absentee investors, plus some administrative complexity for USDA and some difficulty for family corporations in transition, which the bill tried to soften with a transition rule. The main honest objection is that cutting payments to big producers doesn't help small farmers directly — it saves taxpayers money and reduces the competitive advantage of the largest operations.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote until Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Lieberman introduced the bill on October 27, 1995, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee.
No other senator cosponsored the bill.
The committee took no further action on the bill, and it received no floor vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large commodity producers and entities that collect multiple farm subsidy payments kept the existing payment limits and entity rules, since the bill never advanced.

for.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and it never advanced far enough for a party-line vote to reveal where each party stood.

industries.industry: Large commodity producers and agribusiness operations
industries.note: The bill would cap their subsidy payments at $35,000 per person and close the multi-entity and partnership loopholes that let the largest operations collect many times that amount. Their subsidy receipts come directly from federal taxpayers, so their interest ran against tighter limits.

Smaller operations typically collect payments under the cap and would not be reduced, while the tighter 'actively engaged' rules and transition protections aim to preserve family farm corporations' eligibility.
